request.system:
You review a blog article an online shop is about to publish. You did not write it. You see the shop, the topic and the search it targets, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), and the article. Sentences about products end with the facts they rest on in brackets; [G] marks a sentence the writer says is general knowledge.

Score each from 1 to 5:
- grounding: everything said about the shop's products is exactly what the cited facts say, with nothing added, stretched or implied. One product claim the facts do not support caps this at 2. No invented experience ("we tested", customer stories), statistics or studies.
- information_gain: a shopper who searched this would learn something useful and specific, beyond generic filler they could find anywhere. Padding, repetition and vague praise lower it.
- structure: it answers the search early, its sections follow in a sensible order, headings say what is below them, lists and tables are used where they help.
- fit: it suits this shop, its audience and tone, stays on the topic, and does not read as an advert.
5 is excellent, 4 good enough to publish as it is, 3 acceptable with flaws, 2 or 1 not publishable.

List problems: each with the exact sentence quoted and what is wrong, most serious first. Leave the list empty if there are none.

For each numbered general-knowledge sentence you are given, say whether every number in it is well established and uncontroversial general knowledge that needs no source (accepted true), or not (false), with a short reason.

<article>
Title: How to Use a French Press: A Step-by-Step Guide to a Clean, Full-Bodied Cup

To use a French press, weigh about 1 g of coffee for every 15–16 g of water, grind it coarse, pour water just off the boil, steep for about 4 minutes, skim the crust, then plunge slowly and pour out every drop at once [G]. Get those variables right and you get the heavy, rounded body the method is known for, without a layer of sludge at the bottom of the mug. The rest of this guide covers each step and the reasoning behind it, plus how to keep your press clean.

## Why the French press tastes the way it does

A French press is an immersion brewer. Instead of water flowing through a bed of coffee, as it does in pour-over, all of the grounds sit in all of the water for the whole brew. Extraction is even and forgiving, and it is controlled mostly by grind size and time.

The other half of the character comes from the filter. A paper filter traps coffee oils and very fine particles, while a metal mesh lets a good share of them through. Those oils and fines are what give French press coffee its weight and texture. Handled badly, the same fines turn the cup muddy and gritty, which is why grind and technique matter so much.

Our [French Press](P1) is an immersion brewer made by Fernhill, with a borosilicate glass beaker held in a stainless steel frame [F2, F3, F4, F5]. Its plunger carries a four-layer mesh filter to separate the grounds from the finished coffee [F7].

{{P1}}

## What you need: ratio, dose and batch size

A reliable starting ratio is 1:15 to 1:16 by weight [G]. That works out at roughly 62–67 g of coffee per litre of water [G]. Use the stronger end if you like a dense, syrupy cup and the weaker end for something lighter and easier to drink.

Weigh both the coffee and the water rather than using scoops. Bean size, density and roast level all change how much coffee a scoop holds, so volume measures make it hard to repeat a good brew. A kitchen scale makes the whole process consistent.

Our [French Press](P1) has a capacity of 1 litre and makes about 4 mugs [F1, F6]. You do not have to fill it every time; scale the dose to the water instead:

- 250 ml of water: about 16–17 g of coffee [G].
- 500 ml of water: about 31–33 g of coffee [G].
- 750 ml of water: about 47–50 g of coffee [G].
- 1 litre of water: about 62–67 g of coffee [G].

## Grind coarse and grind fresh

Grind size is the single biggest lever in French press brewing. A coarse grind, roughly like coarse sea salt, slows extraction so the coffee does not turn bitter over a long steep. Just as important, coarse particles are too big to pass through the mesh, so fewer fines end up suspended in your cup.

Evenness matters as much as size. A blade grinder smashes beans into a mix of boulders and dust, and that dust slips straight through the filter. A burr grinder cuts beans to a far more uniform size, which gives a cleaner cup and more predictable extraction. Grind just before you brew, too: ground coffee loses aroma quickly, and the difference is obvious in a method that showcases body and flavour as directly as this one.

Our [Hand Grinder](P2) is a manual grinder with 38 mm hardened stainless steel conical burrs [F11, F12]. It has external click adjustment with 30 settings, running from espresso at the fine end to French press at the coarse end [F13, F14]. It holds 25 g of beans [F15]. To compare other options, browse our [grinders](L2).

{{P2}}

## Step by step: brewing your French press

With your coffee weighed and ground, the brew itself is simple. The details below are what separate a clean cup from a muddy one.

- **Preheat the beaker.** Fill it with hot water, swirl, and discard. A warm beaker keeps the brew temperature stable instead of pulling heat out of the water.
- **Add the grounds.** Tip them in and give the beaker a gentle shake to level the bed.
- **Pour water just off the boil.** Aim for roughly 93–96 °C [G]. Without a thermometer, letting a boiled kettle rest for about 30 seconds gets you close [G]. Pour steadily so all the grounds are soaked.
- **Stir gently.** A brief stir makes sure no dry clumps remain. Set the lid on with the plunger pulled all the way up to hold in the heat.
- **Steep.** Leave it for about 4 minutes [G]. A crust of grounds and foam will form on the surface.
- **Break the crust and skim.** Give the crust a gentle stir so most of it sinks, then spoon off the remaining foam and floating grounds. This removes much of the fine material that would otherwise end up in your cup.
- **Let it settle (optional).** For an even cleaner result, wait a few more minutes so the fines drift to the bottom. Extraction slows a lot once the grounds have sunk, so the cup gets clearer rather than harsher.
- **Plunge slowly.** Press the plunger down gently and stop just above the settled grounds. On our [French Press](P1), the four-layer mesh filter does this separating [F7]. Forcing any plunger down fast stirs up the bed and pushes fines through the mesh.
- **Pour it all out at once.** Decant every drop into mugs or a carafe straight away. In an immersion brewer, coffee left sitting on the grounds keeps extracting and turns bitter. Leave the last spoonful in the beaker, where the heaviest sediment collects.

## Choosing beans for the French press

Almost any coffee can be brewed in a French press, but some profiles suit the method especially well. Medium roasts with chocolate and caramel notes sit comfortably with the heavy body of immersion, and the extra texture makes them taste rounder and sweeter. A washed coffee tends to give a clean, sweet base that stays clear even with the oils and fines a mesh filter lets through.

Our [Colombia Huila](P3) fits that profile: it is a washed-process, medium roast coffee with tasting notes of red apple, caramel and milk chocolate [F19, F28, F30]. It is a single-origin coffee from Fernhill Roastery and comes in 250 g and 1 kg bags [F21, F22, F23]. You can find more single origins in our [coffee beans](L3) collection.

{{P3}}

### Adjusting the cup

Once you have a baseline, taste and adjust. Change one thing at a time so you know what made the difference.

| What you taste | Likely cause | What to change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sour, thin, sharp | Under-extraction | Grind a little finer or steep a little longer |
| Bitter, dry, harsh | Over-extraction | Grind a little coarser or steep a little shorter |
| Muddy, gritty | Too many fines | Grind coarser, skim the crust, plunge more slowly |
| Weak but balanced | Dose too low | Use more coffee for the same water |

## Cleaning and care

A French press stays good only if it stays clean. Tip spent grounds into the compost or the bin rather than the sink, where they build up in pipes. Rinse the mesh filter under running water after every brew so grounds do not dry into it.

All parts of our [French Press](P1) come apart for cleaning [F8]. Take the plunger and filter fully apart regularly and wash each piece in warm, soapy water. Coffee oils trapped between the mesh layers turn rancid over time and give later brews a stale, bitter edge, even when the press looks clean from the outside.

The borosilicate glass beaker of our [French Press](P1) is also replaceable if it ever breaks [F4, F9].

## Beyond hot brew: cold brew by immersion

The same immersion principle works with cold water. Coarse coffee steeped for many hours in the fridge produces a smooth, low-acidity concentrate that you dilute to taste. You can do this in a French press, but it ties up your brewer and only makes a modest batch.

Our [Cold Brew Jar](P5) is an immersion brewer that makes 1.5 litres of concentrate, with a recommended steep of 12 to 18 hours in the fridge [F43, F48, F51]. It has an airtight lid and fits in a fridge door, which makes it practical if you keep cold brew on hand regularly [F49, F50]. See the full range in our [immersion brewers](L4) collection.

Whichever way you brew, the fundamentals carry over: weigh your coffee, grind coarse and even, control your time, and separate the coffee from the grounds as soon as it is ready.
